descriptionChirho: The core physical sense of falling or collapsing, covering all Qal inflections where the subject physically falls to the ground. Arabic consistently uses سَقَطَ (saqaṭa) 'to fall' and its imperfect يَسْقُطُ, matching the basic intransitive meaning. Korean distinguishes 떨어졌다 'fell/dropped' and 쓰러졌다 'collapsed/toppled', but these are sub-aspects of the same physical falling. Swahili uses the base verb -anguka 'fall' across tenses (akaanguka, ataanguka, ameanguka) with no derivational shift. Hindi गिरा/गिरे/गिरेंगे are simple tense variants of the same girna 'to fall'.

labelChirho: Qal: fall in state / lie fallen (participle)
descriptionChirho: The stative-participial sense where the subject is in a state of having fallen or lying prostrate, not the event of falling itself. Arabic uses the active participle سَاقِطٌ (sāqiṭ) 'fallen one / one lying fallen'. Korean 쓰러진 'collapsed (adjectival)' and 엎드러져 있었다 'was lying prostrate' emphasize the resultant state. Swahili ameanguka (perfect aspect) and amelala 'was lying' confirm a stative reading. Hindi गिरा हुआ (girā huā) is the explicit stative participle 'in a fallen state'.

A specialized military sense where נפל means 'to desert' or 'defect to the enemy side'. Arabic uses an entirely different root هَرَبَ (haraba) 'to flee/desert' and its participle هَارِبٌ (hārib) / plural الهاربين, proving this is a genuinely distinct lexical sense, not merely contextual usage of 'fall'. Korean uses 투항한 'surrendered/defected' and 넘어간 'crossed over (to enemy)', both distinct from simple 'fall'. Swahili uses walijisalimisha 'they surrendered themselves' and waliokimbia 'those who fled', again totally different from -anguka. Hindi भाग गए (bhāg gaye) 'they fled' and भागेड़ू (bhāgeṛū) 'deserter' confirm the distinct sense.

A specialized sense where נפל indicates getting down from a mount or descending, distinct from accidental falling. Arabic uses نَزَلَ (nazala) 'to descend/dismount' rather than سَقَطَ, confirming a separate lexical sense. Korean 내렸다 (naeryeotda) 'descended/dismounted' is distinct from any 'fall' verb. Swahili akashuka 'descended' uses the verb -shuka 'to come down' rather than -anguka. Hindi उतरा/उतरी (utarā/utarī) 'descended' is a completely different verb from girna 'to fall'.

Used when falling upon someone in a hostile sense, i.e., to attack or raid. Arabic وَقَعَ (waqaʿa) 'to fall upon/befall' appears in some of these contexts (distinct from سَقَطَ). Korean 덮쳤다 (deopchyeotda) 'attacked/raided' is clearly different from simple falling. Swahili wakashambulia 'they attacked' uses -shambulia 'to attack'. Hindi गिर पड़े (gir paṛe) can carry the nuance of 'falling upon' someone.

labelChirho: Qal: be allotted / fall as inheritance
descriptionChirho: A sense where land or portions 'fall' to someone as inheritance or allotment by lot. Arabic يُلْقَوْنَ (yulqawna, passive of ألقى) 'they are cast/allotted' shows the lot-casting framework. Korean 떨어질 것이다 retains literal 'fall' but the context is allocation. Swahili watarithi 'they will inherit' uses a completely different verb -rithi 'to inherit', confirming the distinct semantic domain. This is the intransitive counterpart to the Hifil 'cast lots / allot' sense.

labelChirho: Hitpael: prostrate oneself / fall down in worship
descriptionChirho: The Hitpael reflexive stem indicates deliberate self-prostration, typically in worship or reverence, not accidental falling. Arabic uses سَقَطْتُ (saqaṭtu) but also سَاجِدًا (sājidan) 'prostrating in worship' for the participle, linking to the root سجد 'worship/prostrate'. Korean consistently uses 엎드렸다 (eopdeureotda) 'prostrated oneself' and 엎드리며 (eopdeurimyeo) 'while prostrating'. Swahili uses the reflexive causative -jiangusha 'to throw oneself down' (nilijiangusha, akijiangusha), with the reflexive -ji- prefix confirming deliberate action. Spanish me postré 'I prostrated myself' is explicitly reflexive.

labelChirho: Hifil: cause to fall / strike down
descriptionChirho: The basic Hifil causative meaning: to cause someone or something to fall, knock down, or strike down. Arabic uses the Form IV causative أَسْقَطَ (asqaṭa) / يُسْقِطُ (yusqiṭu) 'to cause to fall', the morphological causative of سَقَطَ, and also أَوْقَعَ (awqaʿa) 'to cause to befall'. Korean uses 떨어뜨리다 (tteoreotteurida) 'to make fall/drop' and 쓰러뜨리다 (ssureotteurida) 'to topple/knock down', both causative derivations. Swahili uses the causative -angusha 'to cause to fall' (from -anguka), with forms like akaangusha, nitamwangusha, kuangusha. Hindi गिराना (girānā) is the explicit causative of गिरना.

The Hifil used specifically for casting lots or throwing objects, where the action is a deliberate projective throw rather than causing someone to fall. Arabic consistently uses أَلْقَى (alqā) 'to throw/cast' and its forms يُلْقِي / أَلْقُوا / نُلْقِي / تُلْقِي, a completely different root from أَسْقَطَ, proving a distinct sense. Korean uses 던졌다 (deonjyeotda) 'threw' and 제비를 뽑으라 'draw lots', distinct from 'cause to fall'. Swahili uses -piga kura 'to cast lots' (wakapiga kura, tulipiga) and -tupa 'to throw' (alitupa, itupe), neither of which is -angusha. Hindi डालना (ḍālnā) 'to throw/cast' and चिट्ठी डालना 'to cast lots' are distinct from गिराना 'to cause to fall'.

labelChirho: Hifil: allot / divide land by lot
descriptionChirho: A specialized Hifil sense where casting lots results in the distribution or allotment of land or inheritance. Arabic uses أَقْسِمْ (aqsim) 'divide!' from the root قسم 'to divide/apportion' and إلقاء (ilqāʾ) 'casting' in the context of land division, distinct from both أَسْقَطَ and the simple أَلْقَى of lot-throwing. Korean 나누다 (nanuda) 'to divide/apportion' is used rather than 던지다 'to throw'. Swahili uses -gawanya/-gawia 'to distribute/divide' (waigawanye, akawagawia, mtaigawanya) rather than -piga kura or -angusha. Hindi बाँटना (bāṁṭnā) 'to distribute' confirms a distinct sense from mere lot-casting.

A rare Hifil sense where נפל refers to the womb 'casting forth' or giving birth, a biological metaphor of causing to fall out. Arabic uses تُخْرِجُ (tukhrijū) 'she brings out/produces' from the root خرج 'to go out', entirely different from any fall vocabulary. Korean 내어놓으리라 (naeeonoheurira) 'shall put forth/produce'. Swahili itawazaa 'it will give birth to them' uses -zaa 'to give birth'. Hindi गिराएगी (girāegī) retains the causative of 'fall' but the context is parturition.

A Hifil sense of allowing something to fall or dropping it, with a nuance of neglect or letting go. Arabic uses تُهْمِلْ (tuhmil) 'to neglect' from the root همل, a completely different semantic field from causing to fall. Korean 빠뜨리지 (ppatteuriji) 'do not let drop/miss'. Swahili uses neno 'word' in the context of not letting a word fall to the ground. Hindi छोड़ना (choṛnā) 'to let go/release' confirms the sense of permissive rather than active causation. This is semantically distinct from the forceful 'strike down' Hifil.

A specialized Hifil sense of felling or cutting down trees. Arabic uses يَقْطَعُونَ (yaqṭaʿūna) / تَقْطَعُونَ (taqṭaʿūna) 'they cut down' from the root قطع 'to cut', a completely different root from any falling vocabulary. Korean 넘어뜨리다 (neomeotteurida) 'to topple/knock over' retains a causative-fall sense but is applied specifically to trees. Swahili -uangusha 'to fell' uses the causative of -anguka. Hindi गिराना (girānā) 'to cause to fall' is applied to trees.
